sections.heading: What is high cholesterol?
sections.body: High cholesterol, also called hypercholesterolaemia, means there is too much cholesterol in the blood. High cholesterol does not usually cause symptoms, so a blood test is the only way to find out whether someone has it. Cholesterol travels in the blood in different forms. HDL cholesterol is often called the good type because it carries excess cholesterol back to the liver, while non-HDL cholesterol is the bad type and can build up in the arteries, the British Heart Foundation says. Having too much cholesterol in the blood can narrow the arteries as fatty material builds up, which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. The NHS describes heart and blood vessel problems caused by high cholesterol as cardiovascular disease. Triglycerides are another type of fat in the blood, and they can also add to fatty build-up in the arteries. Heart UK says anyone can have a higher cholesterol level, even people who are slim, eat well and are physically active.

sections.heading: What causes high cholesterol?
sections.body:
Heart UK says lifestyle, genes and overall health can all have an effect on cholesterol, and these can add up. Lifestyle factors include drinking more alcohol than recommended, excess weight (especially around the middle), smoking, a diet high in saturated fat and low physical activity. The British Heart Foundation lists the main sources of saturated fat as fatty meats, full fat dairy products such as butter and cream, palm and coconut oil, and processed foods such as biscuits, cakes and pastries. The British Heart Foundation says that cholesterol in foods such as eggs and shellfish has only a minimal effect for most people, while saturated fat matters more.

High cholesterol can run in families. Heart UK says the risk is higher for people with a close relative, such as a parent or sibling, who has had high cholesterol or cardiovascular disease. The NHS says people are more likely to develop high cholesterol if they are over 50, male, past the menopause, or of South Asian or sub-Saharan African origin. Heart UK says familial hypercholesterolaemia is a common inherited condition caused by a change in one gene, which makes the liver less able to remove excess LDL cholesterol. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is the most common genetic cause of early cardiovascular disease, the Genomics Education Programme says.

sections.heading: How is high cholesterol diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP may suggest a cholesterol test depending on factors such as age, weight and other conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes. The NHS Health Check, offered to some adults without certain existing conditions, includes a cholesterol test. The NHS says a cholesterol test can also be done at some pharmacies, sometimes for a fee. A lipid profile blood test measures HDL cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol, the cholesterol ratio, triglycerides and total cholesterol. The British Heart Foundation says a GP can use the results to say which targets apply, because these depend on individual risk.

Other causes of high cholesterol, such as diabetes or an underactive thyroid, are excluded first when familial hypercholesterolaemia is suspected. A scoring guide such as the Simon Broome criteria may be used, and genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis in some cases. Familial hypercholesterolaemia can cause lumps around the knuckles, knees or the back of the ankle, a pale ring around the coloured part of the eye, or small yellow patches on the skin around the eyes. NICE advises two measurements of LDL cholesterol because results can vary for biological and analytical reasons. NICE recommends referral to a specialist lipid clinic to confirm the diagnosis, counsel the person and start cascade testing, which means testing relatives.

sections.heading: How is high cholesterol treated?
sections.body:
Treatment starts with lifestyle changes such as healthier eating and more activity, and some people also need medicine. The NHS says that for some people lifestyle changes alone are not enough. Statins are the most common medicine for high cholesterol, usually taken as a daily tablet and often for the long term. The NHS says most people can take statins, but they are not suitable for everyone, for example people with severe liver disease or who are pregnant. Atorvastatin is a statin used to lower cholesterol and to prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes. The NHS says atorvastatin works by stopping the liver from making cholesterol. NICE guidance on lipid modification recommends atorvastatin as the statin to offer for preventing cardiovascular disease.

If statins do not suit a person or are not enough, the NHS lists other medicines such as ezetimibe, bempedoic acid and some injected medicines. The NHS says ezetimibe is prescribed if someone cannot take statins or a statin is not working for them, and it reduces the cholesterol absorbed from food. For familial hypercholesterolaemia, NHS England guidance describes lipid-lowering medicine, which will be life-long, as the first line of treatment.

sections.heading: Living with high cholesterol and getting help
sections.body:
The NHS advises eating less saturated fat, choosing unsaturated fats such as those in oily fish, olive oil, nuts and seeds, and being more active. The NHS also advises stopping smoking and cutting back on alcohol. Heart UK says regular aerobic exercise that raises the heart rate can improve LDL levels and lower triglycerides. Heart UK also says that losing weight can help raise HDL cholesterol, and that stopping smoking can too. Heart UK says losing excess weight and getting regular exercise can often lower triglyceride levels.

A GP appointment is the usual route for a cholesterol check, and the GP reads the result alongside other risk factors. Sudden chest pain or signs of a stroke need an emergency call to 999.

coeliac-disease.name: Coeliac disease
coeliac-disease.definition: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system reacts to gluten and damages the lining of the small bowel.
coeliac-disease.overview: Coeliac disease is a lifelong autoimmune condition in which the immune system reacts to gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley and rye. The reaction damages the lining of the small bowel, so the body cannot absorb nutrients well. NHS inform estimates that it affects about 1 in every 100 people, and many of them have not been diagnosed. Symptoms vary widely from person to person, and some people have none. A gluten-free diet is the main treatment.
causes: It is an autoimmune reaction in which the immune system responds abnormally to gluten and damages the lining of the small bowel.
Genes that make a person more likely to develop it are involved, and the exact trigger is not yet known.
Something in the environment seems to set off the condition in some people who carry these genes.
riskFactors: Having a close relative with coeliac disease raises the chance of having it, and NICE recommends testing first-degree relatives.
Type 1 diabetes is linked with coeliac disease, probably because both share a genetic risk.
NICE also recommends testing for people with autoimmune thyroid disease.
signs: Children may grow more slowly than expected or reach puberty later.
An itchy, blistering rash called dermatitis herpetiformis can appear, often on the elbows, knees and buttocks.
complications: Poor absorption of nutrients can lead to iron deficiency anaemia and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia.
Osteoporosis, in which bones become weaker, is among the conditions that poor absorption can cause.
Small bowel cancer and small bowel lymphoma are linked to the condition, although most people with it do not develop them.
In some people the spleen works less well, which can make infections more likely.
Delayed puberty in children and low birth weight in newborn babies have also been described.
Rarely, symptoms continue despite a strict gluten-free diet, which is called refractory coeliac disease.
coeliac-disease.diagnosis: Diagnosis usually starts with a blood test for coeliac antibodies arranged by a GP. A positive blood test is followed by referral to a gastroenterologist, who may arrange a biopsy of the small bowel to confirm the diagnosis. Gluten needs to stay in the diet until testing is finished, because stopping it first can give a false negative result.
coeliac-disease.treatment: There is no cure, but the NHS says a gluten-free diet should help control symptoms and prevent long-term complications. All sources of gluten are avoided for life. Bread, pasta, cereals, biscuits and cakes are avoided unless labelled gluten-free. NICE recommends a yearly review of symptoms and how well the diet is working.
coeliac-disease.prevention: Following a gluten-free diet is described as helping to prevent the long-term complications of the condition.
coeliac-disease.seekCare: A GP appointment is the usual route for people with ongoing unexplained gut symptoms, unexplained weight loss, long-lasting tiredness or unexplained anaemia, since the GP can arrange the blood test. For people already diagnosed, NICE advises a review when symptoms continue despite excluding gluten.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of coeliac disease?
sections.body:
Coeliac disease commonly causes diarrhoea, stomach aches and bloating. Indigestion and constipation can also occur. The NHS lists other effects, including tiredness, unplanned weight loss and mouth ulcers, as well as an itchy rash.

Nerve problems can occur, such as numbness and tingling in the hands and feet, and difficulties with co-ordination, balance and speech. Symptoms vary widely between people. Coeliac UK describes the condition as multi-system, which means symptoms can affect any area of the body, and its symptoms can be mistaken for those of other conditions.

The NHS says that although dermatitis herpetiformis is not a symptom of coeliac disease, a person with an autoimmune response to gluten may develop this itchy, blistering rash. It typically appears on the elbows, knees and buttocks. Some people have no symptoms at all. Children with the condition may not grow at the expected rate, or may be late to reach puberty, according to NHS inform.

sections.heading: What causes coeliac disease?
sections.body:
Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition. NICE describes gluten from wheat, barley and rye as the dietary trigger that sets off an abnormal immune response in the lining of the gut. The reaction damages the lining of the small bowel, which is where nutrients are absorbed.

NHS 111 Wales says the exact trigger is unclear, but genes and the environment both seem to play a part. The condition is strongly tied to certain variants of a group of genes called HLA-DQ. Something in the environment seems to set the condition off in some people who carry them.

First-degree relatives of a person with coeliac disease are more likely to have it themselves, and NICE recommends testing them. Type 1 diabetes is linked with coeliac disease, and Coeliac UK attributes this to a shared genetic predisposition. NICE also recommends testing for people with type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease when they are diagnosed with those conditions.

sections.heading: How is coeliac disease diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS advises testing for people with any one of a list of symptoms, such as ongoing unexplained gut symptoms or unexplained weight loss. NICE recommends offering a blood test to people with persistent unexplained abdominal or gastrointestinal symptoms, and considering it for people with unexplained neurological symptoms, particularly peripheral neuropathy.

The two main methods are a blood test and a biopsy. A GP usually arranges the first blood test, which looks for coeliac antibodies. After a positive result the GP refers the person to a gastroenterologist, who may arrange more blood tests or a biopsy of the small bowel.

The NHS says gluten must stay in the diet until testing is finished, because testing is only reliable in people who have been eating it. Stopping gluten first can cause a false negative result and delay diagnosis. NICE advises that a person should not start a gluten-free diet until a specialist confirms the diagnosis, even if the blood test is positive.

NHS inform notes that it is sometimes possible to have coeliac disease without antibodies in the blood, and that there is not enough evidence that home test kits are reliable.

sections.heading: How is coeliac disease treated?
sections.body:
The main treatment is avoiding gluten. The NHS says all sources of gluten are avoided for life. There is no cure, but following a gluten-free diet should help control symptoms and prevent the long-term complications of the condition. Foods such as bread, pasta, cereals, biscuits and cakes are avoided unless they are labelled gluten-free.

The NHS says symptoms should improve considerably within weeks of starting a gluten-free diet, although full healing of the gut can take up to a few years. The rash of dermatitis herpetiformis can take longer to clear than other symptoms. In that case the NHS says a medicine called dapsone is usually used, and regular blood tests may be needed to check for anaemia, which is one of its side effects.

The NHS says oats contain a protein called avenin that suits most people with coeliac disease but may trigger symptoms in a few. Oats are often contaminated during processing, so those not labelled gluten-free are avoided. Anyone who wants to add oats can first talk to a healthcare professional. NICE recommends an annual review of symptoms and of how well the gluten-free diet is working.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
Poor absorption of nutrients, called malabsorption, can lead to a shortage of vitamins and minerals. The NHS lists iron deficiency anaemia and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia among the results. It also lists osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker. Coeliac UK says that early diagnosis in childhood helps bones reach normal mass, and NICE recommends testing people with reduced bone mineral density.

The NHS names small bowel cancer, small bowel lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma as cancers linked to coeliac disease, but most people with the condition do not develop them. After some time on a gluten-free diet the risk returns to that of the general population. NHS 111 Wales says the spleen can work less well in some people, which raises the risk of infection.

Some people keep having symptoms despite a gluten-free diet. NICE advises reviewing the symptoms and checking for continued exposure to gluten, including hidden gluten. If symptoms persist despite a strict diet and no other cause is found, it may be refractory coeliac disease. Coeliac UK says this is very rare, and the NHS says a specialist may use steroid or immunosuppressant medicines.

faqs.q: Can coeliac disease be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for coeliac disease. Following a gluten-free diet for life should help control symptoms and prevent long-term complications. The NHS says symptoms should improve considerably within weeks, although full healing of the gut can take longer, up to a few years.

faqs.q: Should I stop eating gluten before being tested?
faqs.a: The NHS says gluten should stay in the diet until testing is finished, because testing is only reliable in people who have been eating it. Stopping it can cause a false negative result and delay diagnosis. NICE advises against starting a gluten-free diet until a specialist confirms the diagnosis. A GP can discuss any worries about this.

faqs.q: Does coeliac disease run in families?
faqs.a: Genes play a part, and NHS 111 Wales says something in the environment also seems to trigger the condition. NICE notes that first-degree relatives of a person with coeliac disease are more likely to have it, and it recommends testing them. Not everyone who carries the genes develops the condition.

faqs.q: Can coeliac disease cause a skin rash?
faqs.a: The NHS says that although it is not a symptom of coeliac disease, a person with an autoimmune response to gluten may develop an itchy, blistering rash called dermatitis herpetiformis, usually on the elbows, knees and buttocks. If a gluten-free diet is slow to clear the rash, the NHS says a medicine called dapsone is usually used.

faqs.q: What happens at an annual review?
faqs.a: NICE recommends that people with coeliac disease are offered a review once a year. The clinician reviews symptoms and considers whether the diet and how well the gluten-free diet is being followed need assessing. Coeliac UK notes that warning signs such as ongoing diarrhoea, stomach pain, weight loss or tiredness need prompt review.

hepatitis-c.name: Hepatitis C
hepatitis-c.definition: Hepatitis C is an infection with a virus that causes inflammation of the liver, which can damage the liver over time.
hepatitis-c.overview: Hepatitis C is a virus that causes inflammation of the liver, and over time the inflamed liver can become damaged. Most people with hepatitis C have no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it. It is spread through contact with infected blood. It is diagnosed with a blood test, and treatment is a short course of antiviral tablets. Without treatment it can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
causes: Hepatitis C is caused by a virus that is spread through contact with infected blood.
Casual contact does not spread the virus, and it is not passed on through breast milk, food or water, according to WHO.
riskFactors: Medical or dental equipment that is reused or not properly sterilised, especially needles and syringes, according to WHO.
Having had a blood transfusion in the UK in the past.
Being the baby of a mother who has hepatitis C.
Having a home-made or overseas tattoo, or a tattoo or piercing done with equipment that was not sterile.
signs: Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice) may be seen.
complications: Cirrhosis, which is scarring of the liver.
Liver failure.
Liver cancer.
Complications may come more quickly with regular alcohol use or with hepatitis B or HIV as well.
hepatitis-c.diagnosis: Hepatitis C is diagnosed using two blood tests, an antibody test and a PCR test. The antibody test shows past exposure, while a positive PCR test means the infection is current. Tests are available through GPs, sexual health clinics and drug treatment services.
hepatitis-c.treatment: Treatment is with antiviral medicines. The medicines now used are tablets called direct-acting antivirals, taken daily for 8 to 12 weeks, according to the NHS. A specialist usually manages treatment.
hepatitis-c.prevention: There is no vaccine for hepatitis C. Ways to reduce the risk include not sharing drug-injecting equipment, razors or toothbrushes.
hepatitis-c.seekCare: The NHS advises a GP appointment for anyone who has symptoms or thinks they could have been infected. The British Liver Trust recommends testing for people who have ever injected drugs or had a home-made or overseas tattoo, even if they feel well.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of hepatitis C?
sections.body:
Most people with hepatitis C have no symptoms. Because of this, many people do not know they have the virus. When symptoms do appear, they can take weeks, months or even years to start. Early symptoms can include a high temperature, tiredness, tummy pain, loss of appetite, feeling or being sick, and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, which is called jaundice. NHS 111 Wales says around 1 in 5 people who get symptoms also develop jaundice.

The British Liver Trust says about 8 in 10 people with a new, or acute, infection have no symptoms. Later on, untreated infection can bring tiredness, itchy skin, low mood, and problems with memory or concentration, the NHS says. These symptoms look like those of other illnesses, so the only way to know whether hepatitis C is the cause is to have a blood test.

sections.heading: How is hepatitis C spread?
sections.body:
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with infected blood, mainly blood-to-blood contact. In the UK, the NHS says sharing injecting equipment is the main route. It says people who inject drugs, including performance-enhancing drugs such as anabolic steroids, are at the highest risk. Other routes it lists include sharing razors or toothbrushes, unsterilised tattoo or piercing equipment, and blood transfusions in the UK in the past. WHO also lists the reuse or poor sterilisation of medical equipment, especially needles and syringes, and the transfusion of unscreened blood.

A baby can catch the virus from an infected mother. GOV.UK guidance for GPs says the chance is higher when the mother also has HIV. The NHS describes sexual transmission as rare. WHO says the virus is not spread through casual contact such as hugging, kissing or sharing food and drink. It is also not spread through breast milk, food or water.

The British Liver Trust recommends testing for people who have ever injected drugs or had a home-made or overseas tattoo, even if they have no symptoms.

sections.heading: How is hepatitis C diagnosed?
sections.body:
Hepatitis C is diagnosed using two blood tests, an antibody test and a PCR test. The antibody test shows whether a person has ever been exposed to the virus. A positive PCR test shows the infection is current. The NHS says results usually come back within 2 weeks. The British Liver Trust describes the same order, with a positive antibody test followed by an RNA test to confirm active infection.

GP surgeries, sexual health clinics, genito-urinary medicine clinics and drug treatment services all offer testing. People aged 18 or over in England can also order a free home test kit from the NHS. The test involves pricking a finger and sending the blood off to be tested.

If hepatitis C is diagnosed, the person is usually referred to a specialist for treatment. The NHS says the doctor will also assess the liver for damage, either with a blood test or with a scan called a fibroscan.

sections.heading: How is hepatitis C treated?
sections.body:
Hepatitis C is treated with antiviral medicines. The NHS says these are tablets taken every day for 8 to 12 weeks, and that it is important to finish the course for treatment to work. The British Liver Trust calls the medicines direct-acting antivirals. The NHS says most people have very few side effects, or none.

The NHS says these medicines cure 9 out of 10 patients, and another NHS source gives a figure of more than 95 in 100. WHO also reports that direct-acting antivirals cure more than 95 in 100 people. A blood test at the end of treatment shows whether the virus has cleared, and a second blood test follows 12 or 24 weeks after treatment stops. MedlinePlus describes a cure as the virus no longer being detectable in the blood 12 weeks or more after treatment.

With a new infection, a clinician may wait to see whether it becomes long-lasting before starting treatment. NHS England says treatment is also available for children aged 3 and over.

sections.heading: What is the outlook for hepatitis C?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says most people who are infected go on to have long-lasting, or chronic, hepatitis C unless they are treated. Chronic infection often goes unnoticed until liver damage appears, which can happen decades after infection. Without treatment, it can lead to scarring of the liver, called cirrhosis, as well as liver failure and liver cancer. MedlinePlus says early diagnosis and treatment can prevent these complications. The NHS says complications may come more quickly with regular alcohol use or with hepatitis B or HIV as well.

The British Liver Trust says that if the virus is stopped early enough, the liver can start to heal. It advises people who are recovering to drink only a very small amount of alcohol, and says a doctor may advise no alcohol at all if liver damage is more severe.

The NHS says successful treatment does not give protection against getting hepatitis C again, so catching it a second time is possible. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.

faqs.q: Can the virus be cleared with treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says antiviral tablets cure 9 out of 10 patients, and WHO reports that direct-acting antivirals cure more than 95 in 100 people. Treatment is a course of daily tablets for 8 to 12 weeks. Blood tests at the end of treatment and again later check whether the virus has cleared. A specialist usually manages treatment.

faqs.q: Does hepatitis C always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. Most people with hepatitis C have no symptoms. Any symptoms that appear can take weeks, months or years to start. The British Liver Trust says about 8 in 10 people with a new infection have no symptoms. Because of this, many people only find out once they get symptoms of liver disease, so testing is recommended for people who may have been exposed.

faqs.q: Can hepatitis C be caught more than once?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says successful treatment does not give protection against getting hepatitis C again, so it can be caught a second time. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C. Ways to lower the risk include not sharing drug-injecting equipment, razors or toothbrushes, which GOV.UK guidance for GPs also advises.

faqs.q: Can hepatitis C be passed on through sex or from mother to baby?
faqs.a: The NHS describes sexual transmission as rare. A baby can catch the virus from an infected mother, and GOV.UK guidance for GPs says the chance is higher when the mother also has HIV. WHO says casual contact does not spread the virus, and it is not passed on through breast milk, food or water.

faqs.q: How can someone get tested for hepatitis C?
faqs.a: Hepatitis C is diagnosed using an antibody blood test and a PCR blood test. GP surgeries, sexual health clinics and drug treatment services offer testing. People aged 18 or over in England can also order a free home kit from the NHS, which involves pricking a finger and sending the blood off to be tested. Results usually come back within 2 weeks.

sinusitis.name: Sinusitis
sinusitis.definition: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, usually caused by an infection.
sinusitis.overview: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, the air-filled spaces in the bones of the face, and it is usually caused by an infection. It is common and usually clears up on its own within 4 weeks. Most often a cold or flu virus spreads to the sinuses from the upper airways, and only a few cases involve bacteria. Antibiotics are rarely needed.
causes: A cold or flu virus spreading to the sinuses from the upper airways is the usual cause.
Only a few cases involve bacteria.
Sinusitis can also follow an inflammatory reaction or an infection with a fungus.
Blocked sinus openings or extra mucus can let germs multiply.
A deviated nasal septum, a nasal bone spur or nasal polyps may block the openings of the sinuses.
riskFactors: A weakened immune system, for example from HIV or chemotherapy.
signs: Mucus from the nose may be coloured.
complications: Complications are very rare.
They include an abscess, a bone infection, meningitis and infection of the tissue around the eye.
Chronic sinusitis can also be linked to a mucocele.
sinusitis.diagnosis: A GP can usually diagnose sinusitis from the symptoms and by looking inside the nose. Scans or other tests may be used if the diagnosis is unclear. Referral to an ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist is considered for severe or repeated cases.
sinusitis.treatment: Most cases clear up on their own, and the NHS suggests rest, plenty of fluids, pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, and saline nasal rinses. A pharmacist or GP may suggest steroid or antihistamine nasal treatments. NICE advises against offering antibiotics to people who have had symptoms for about 10 days or less. An ear, nose and throat specialist may suggest surgery to improve drainage of the sinuses if symptoms do not improve.
sinusitis.prevention: The NHS lists avoiding allergy triggers and not smoking among its suggestions.
sinusitis.seekCare: An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised if someone is very unwell, painkillers do not help or symptoms get worse, or the immune system is weakened. A GP appointment is advised if there is no improvement after 7 days of treatment from a pharmacist or GP, none after 3 weeks of self-care, or the problem keeps coming back. Swelling around the eye or face, blood-stained discharge from the nose or changes in vision need prompt medical review, through the GP the same day or NHS 111.

sections.heading: What is sinusitis?
sections.body:
Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, and it is usually caused by an infection. The NHS describes it as common, and it usually clears up on its own within 4 weeks. MedlinePlus explains that sinusitis results from an inflammatory reaction or an infection with a virus, bacteria or a fungus.

Sinusitis that lasts a long time is called chronic sinusitis. One MedlinePlus page describes it as sinus swelling and symptoms lasting longer than 3 months. Another MedlinePlus page describes it as lasting more than 12 weeks and says it can continue for months or even years. MedlinePlus says the symptoms of chronic sinusitis tend to be milder but last longer than those of a short infection. MedlinePlus lists nasal stuffiness and discharge, a cough that is often worse at night, postnasal drip, facial pressure or pain, headache and tiredness as symptoms of chronic sinusitis.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of sinusitis?
sections.body:
The NHS lists pain and tenderness in the face, a blocked or runny nose and a reduced sense of smell as main symptoms. Coloured mucus from the nose and a fever are also listed. Headache, toothache and bad breath are also listed. In young children, irritability and trouble feeding can appear.

MedlinePlus lists pressure or pain in the face, a stuffy nose with discharge, cough, fever and headache. It also lists mucus running down the back of the throat, known as postnasal drip. A GP can usually diagnose sinusitis from these symptoms, together with a look inside the nose. MedlinePlus advises contacting a health care provider, such as a GP, if symptoms last beyond 10 to 14 days or if a fever develops.

sections.heading: What causes sinusitis?
sections.body:
The NHS says a cold or flu virus spreading to the sinuses from the upper airways is the usual cause. Only a few cases involve bacteria. MedlinePlus says blocked sinus openings or extra mucus can let germs multiply. A deviated nasal septum, a nasal bone spur or nasal polyps may block the openings of the sinuses. It adds that an inflammatory reaction, and not only an infection, can lead to sinusitis.

Several things are linked to a higher chance of sinusitis. The NHS lists allergies, nasal polyps, smoking and a weakened immune system. MedlinePlus adds allergic rhinitis, cystic fibrosis, attending day care and large adenoids. It gives HIV and chemotherapy as reasons for a weakened immune system. The CDC adds a previous cold, seasonal allergies, secondhand smoke and nasal polyps.

sections.heading: How is sinusitis diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
A GP can usually diagnose sinusitis from the symptoms and by looking inside the nose. Scans or other tests may be used if the diagnosis is unclear. Referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist is considered for severe or repeated cases.

For self-care, the NHS suggests rest, plenty of fluids, pain relief and saline nasal rinses. It also suggests avoiding allergy triggers and not smoking. The NHS says pharmacists can offer the same treatments as a GP for sinusitis. A pharmacist or GP may suggest steroid or antihistamine nasal treatments, and steroid nasal sprays or drops are used to reduce swelling in the sinuses.

NICE guideline NG79 covers antibiotic prescribing for acute sinusitis. For people with symptoms for about 10 days or less, it advises against offering an antibiotic. For longer symptoms with no improvement, it describes options that include a nasal corticosteroid, no antibiotic or a back-up prescription, depending on how likely a bacterial cause is. Antibiotics are offered straight away to people who are very unwell, show signs of a more serious illness or have other health conditions. An ear, nose and throat specialist may suggest surgery to improve drainage of the sinuses if symptoms do not improve.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help for sinusitis?
sections.body:
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 if someone is very unwell, painkillers do not help or symptoms get worse, or the immune system is weakened. A GP appointment is advised if there is no improvement after 7 days of treatment from a pharmacist or GP, none after 3 weeks of self-care, or the problem keeps coming back. A GP may refer someone to an ENT specialist if symptoms persist after 3 months of treatment, if it keeps coming back, or if only one side of the face is affected.

Complications are very rare, according to MedlinePlus. It lists an abscess, a bone infection, meningitis and infection of the tissue around the eye. Swelling around the eye or face, blood-stained discharge from the nose or changes in vision need prompt medical review, through the GP the same day or NHS 111. NICE says people with signs of a serious complication should be referred to hospital.

faqs.q: How long does sinusitis last?
faqs.a: The NHS says sinusitis is common and usually clears up on its own within 4 weeks. It advises a GP appointment if there is no improvement after 3 weeks of self-care or after 7 days of treatment from a pharmacist or GP. Chronic sinusitis is described by MedlinePlus as lasting longer than 3 months.

faqs.q: Do I need antibiotics for sinusitis?
faqs.a: Antibiotics are rarely needed, according to the NHS. This is because a virus is the usual cause, and only a few cases involve bacteria. NICE advises against offering them to people with symptoms for about 10 days or less. A clinician may still offer them to someone who is very unwell or has other health conditions.

faqs.q: What can help with the symptoms at home?
faqs.a: The NHS suggests rest, plenty of fluids, pain relief and saline nasal rinses. It also suggests avoiding allergy triggers and not smoking. The NHS says pharmacists can offer the same treatments as a GP for sinusitis, and a pharmacist or GP may suggest steroid or antihistamine nasal treatments.

faqs.q: What are the possible complications?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus calls complications of sinusitis very rare. It lists an abscess, a bone infection, meningitis and infection of the tissue around the eye. Swelling around the eye or face needs prompt medical review, through the GP the same day or NHS 111.

faqs.q: When might a specialist be involved?
faqs.a: A GP may refer someone to an ear, nose and throat specialist if symptoms persist after 3 months of treatment. Referral is also considered if the problem keeps coming back or affects only one side of the face. A specialist may suggest surgery to improve drainage of the sinuses if symptoms do not improve.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for people who are over 65, are pregnant, have a long-term condition such as diabetes or heart, lung or kidney disease, or feel too unwell to do their usual daily activities. The NHS says to see a GP if symptoms last longer than 3 weeks.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of bronchitis?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a cough, chest pain when coughing, shortness of breath, a sore throat, a runny nose and a high temperature. NI Direct, the Northern Ireland public information service, adds that tiredness, headache and aches and pains can also occur. A cough that often brings up mucus is a main symptom, and viruses are the usual cause.

MedlinePlus says the mucus may be clear or yellow-green, and that a fever, when present, is usually low-grade. It also describes chest discomfort and shortness of breath that gets worse with activity. NI Direct says the cough can outlast the other symptoms by several weeks, and MedlinePlus says it can linger for 1 to 4 weeks after the illness clears. Bronchitis often gets better without treatment in around 3 weeks, according to the NHS. In chronic bronchitis, a whistling or squeaky sound when breathing and chest tightness are also reported.

sections.heading: What causes bronchitis?
sections.body:
Bronchitis is inflammation of the airways in the lungs, usually caused by an infection. MedlinePlus describes acute bronchitis as swelling and inflamed tissue in the bronchi, the main passages that carry air to the lungs, and says the swelling can narrow the airways and make it harder to breathe. Acute bronchitis is a short-term infection of the larger airways, which are called the bronchi.

Acute bronchitis is usually caused by a virus, often the same viruses that cause colds and flu. MedlinePlus says these viruses spread through coughing or contact with unwashed hands. Bacteria are a less common cause. Irritants such as tobacco smoke, air pollution, dust and fumes can also trigger it.

Chronic bronchitis is caused by long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke and pollutants. Chronic bronchitis is a different, long-term problem that forms part of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

sections.heading: Who is more at risk, and what can go wrong?
sections.body:
The risk of acute bronchitis is higher in very young and older people, in people with a weakened immune system, and in those with heart or lung disease. A history of smoking, living in a polluted area, crowded living conditions and a history of asthma are also listed as risk factors.

Pneumonia can be a complication, and the risk is higher in people with asthma, COPD or a weakened immune system. Acute respiratory distress syndrome and respiratory failure linked to acute bronchitis have been reported in the medical literature.

Asthma + Lung UK says the main types of chest infection are pneumonia and bronchitis. People with asthma are more likely to get a chest infection, and a chest infection can trigger asthma symptoms and lead to an asthma attack. The charity also says antibiotics only help with bacterial infections, so they will not help a chest infection caused by a virus.

sections.heading: How is bronchitis diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
StatPearls says a chest X-ray in acute bronchitis is usually non-specific and often looks normal, and that it is most useful for telling pneumonia apart. NICE guidance on acute cough sets out when antibiotics are considered, depending on how unwell a person is and whether they are at higher risk of complications.

The NHS suggests resting, drinking plenty of fluids and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever. Honey in a warm drink may soothe the throat, but it is not for babies under 1. NI Direct advises against ibuprofen for people with asthma.

Antibiotics are not routine, but may be offered if the bronchitis is caused by a more serious infection. NICE does not routinely recommend antibiotics for acute bronchitis in people who are not very unwell or at higher risk of complications. NICE says antibiotics shorten a cough by only about half a day on average and can cause side effects, particularly diarrhoea and nausea. For people at higher risk of complications, NICE says an immediate or back-up antibiotic prescription can be considered. The CDC says acute bronchitis usually gets better on its own, without antibiotics.

sections.heading: What is chronic bronchitis?
sections.body:
NHLBI describes chronic bronchitis as lasting at least three months and returning for at least two years in a row. Asthma + Lung UK says it causes the airways to produce a lot of phlegm, which can lead to a long-term cough and breathing problems. It treats chronic bronchitis as part of COPD, a group of lung conditions that also includes emphysema.

Asthma + Lung UK says chronic bronchitis can be managed but cannot be cured. NHLBI says treatment aims to improve breathing and control symptoms, and names quitting smoking, medicines that clear the airways or prevent symptoms getting worse, and oxygen therapy as options. The NHS describes short-acting bronchodilator inhalers as the first treatment for most people with COPD. MedlinePlus describes pulmonary rehabilitation as a programme that helps improve well-being in people with long-term breathing problems.

Stopping smoking is described as the most important step in the care of chronic bronchitis. NHLBI lists avoiding fumes, air pollution and secondhand smoke, and having recommended vaccines such as the yearly flu vaccine, as ways to lower the chance of getting bronchitis or of getting it again.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help?
sections.body:
The NHS says to see a GP if symptoms last longer than 3 weeks. NICE says people should be told that a cough can last up to 3 or 4 weeks without needing an antibiotic, and to seek help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not improve after 3 or 4 weeks, or they become very unwell.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for people who are over 65, are pregnant, have a long-term condition such as diabetes or heart, lung or kidney disease, or feel too unwell to do their usual daily activities. The NHS also lists coughing up blood or blood-stained mucus and feeling short of breath. NI Direct lists blood-streaked mucus and a fever that lasts more than three days as reasons to see a GP.

The NHS says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, their lips or skin turn pale, blue or grey, they suddenly become confused, or a baby is unresponsive or floppy.

faqs.q: How long does bronchitis last?
faqs.a: Bronchitis often gets better without treatment in around 3 weeks, according to the NHS. MedlinePlus says the cough can linger for 1 to 4 weeks after the illness clears. The NHS says to see a GP if symptoms last longer than 3 weeks. NICE says people should be told to seek help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not improve after 3 or 4 weeks, or they become very unwell.

faqs.q: Does bronchitis need antibiotics?
faqs.a: Acute bronchitis is usually caused by a virus, and Asthma + Lung UK says antibiotics only help with bacterial infections. Antibiotics may be offered if the bronchitis is caused by a more serious infection. NICE does not routinely recommend antibiotics for acute bronchitis in people who are not very unwell or at higher risk of complications. The CDC says acute bronchitis usually gets better on its own, without antibiotics.

faqs.q: Is bronchitis the same as COPD?
faqs.a: Acute bronchitis is a short-term infection of the larger airways, which are called the bronchi. Chronic bronchitis is a different, long-term problem that forms part of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). NHLBI describes chronic bronchitis as lasting at least three months and returning for at least two years in a row.

faqs.q: What can help with bronchitis symptoms?
faqs.a: The NHS suggests resting, drinking plenty of fluids and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever. Honey in a warm drink may soothe the throat, but it is not for babies under 1. NI Direct advises against ibuprofen for people with asthma. The NHS says to see a GP if symptoms last longer than 3 weeks.

faqs.q: Can chronic bronchitis be cured?
faqs.a: Asthma + Lung UK says chronic bronchitis can be managed but cannot be cured. It treats chronic bronchitis as part of COPD. NHLBI says treatment aims to improve breathing and control symptoms. Stopping smoking is described as the most important step in the care of chronic bronchitis.

sleep-apnoea.name: Obstructive sleep apnoea
sleep-apnoea.definition: Obstructive sleep apnoea is a condition in which the throat narrows or closes during sleep, so breathing stops and starts again.
sleep-apnoea.overview: In obstructive sleep apnoea, the muscles of the upper airway relax during sleep and the throat narrows or closes. Breathing then stops and restarts. Asthma + Lung UK says about 1 in 20 people have it. Common signs are loud snoring, gasping or choking at night and feeling very tired by day. It is linked with obesity, older age and a family history of the condition.
causes: The muscles of the upper airway relax during sleep, so the throat narrows or closes.
Large tonsils or adenoids are linked with the airway narrowing.
riskFactors: A family history of sleep apnoea
Asthma, especially if overweight, with reflux, or hard to control
signs: A bed partner may notice pauses in breathing, gasping or choking noises, and loud snoring during sleep.
complications: Without treatment, it can contribute to high blood pressure, stroke, type 2 diabetes and heart disease.
Without treatment, it can contribute to low mood.
Daytime tiredness can lead to accidents.
It can make asthma symptoms worse and raise the risk of an asthma attack.
sleep-apnoea.diagnosis: A GP may refer someone to a specialist sleep clinic. The tests can usually be done at home, but sometimes an overnight stay in the clinic is needed. Asthma + Lung UK names respiratory polygraphy and oximetry as the main sleep tests. Doctors judge how severe the condition is by counting the breathing pauses in an hour of the sleep study.
sleep-apnoea.treatment: Lifestyle changes such as losing weight, giving up smoking and drinking less alcohol can help. Many people still need a CPAP machine, which gently pumps air into a mask worn over the nose, or nose and mouth, during sleep. A mandibular advancement device, worn in the mouth to hold the lower jaw forward, is another option. Surgery, such as removing large tonsils, may also be an option.
sleep-apnoea.prevention: The NHS says lifestyle changes such as losing weight, giving up smoking and drinking less alcohol can sometimes help with sleep apnoea.
sleep-apnoea.seekCare: The NHS advises a GP appointment for pauses in breathing during sleep, gasping or choking noises at night, or constant tiredness in the day. GOV.UK says a person with sleep apnoea who has excessive sleepiness must not drive until the sleepiness is free or the symptoms are under control.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea?
sections.body:
Sleep apnoea is when breathing stops and starts during sleep. The NHS lists the main signs as pauses in breathing while asleep, gasping, snorting or choking noises, waking often and loud snoring. Many of these happen while the person is asleep, so they may be noticed by someone else in the room.

The effects carry into the day. People may feel very tired, find it hard to concentrate, have mood changes or wake with a headache. Because it can be hard to tell whether someone has sleep apnoea, the NHS says it can help to ask a bed partner to watch for symptoms. Bringing that person to the appointment is also useful.

Asthma + Lung UK says about 1 in 20 people have obstructive sleep apnoea, and describes it as the most common type of sleep apnoea. Another type, central sleep apnoea, is different: the brain does not send the right signals to the breathing muscles.

sections.heading: What causes it and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
In obstructive sleep apnoea the muscles of the upper airway relax during sleep, so the throat narrows or closes. Breathing then stops and restarts. The NHS links this narrowing with several factors, including obesity, a large neck, older age and a family history of the condition. Alcohol, smoking, large tonsils or adenoids, sleeping on the back and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are also on the NHS list.

These are links rather than proven single causes, and a person can have more than one. Asthma + Lung UK says some people with obstructive sleep apnoea also have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and that having both can make breathing problems during sleep much worse.

Asthma + Lung UK also says people with asthma are more likely to get obstructive sleep apnoea, especially if they are overweight, have gastro-oesophageal reflux disease or have asthma that is difficult to control. It adds that the condition can make asthma symptoms worse and increase the risk of an asthma attack.

sections.heading: How is obstructive sleep apnoea diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP may refer someone to a specialist sleep clinic. The NHS says the tests can usually be done at home, though sometimes an overnight stay in the clinic is needed.

Asthma + Lung UK says a sleep clinic usually takes a history and examines the person. The clinic may ask about sleep, daytime sleepiness, smoking, medicines and family history of sleep disorders. It names pulse oximetry and respiratory polygraphy as the main sleep tests. Oximetry records the oxygen level in the blood and the heart rate, using a small clip on a fingertip or earlobe. Respiratory polygraphy records more, including breathing, oxygen level, heart rate, movement and snoring sounds. If the result is not clear, a fuller study called polysomnography may be needed.

NICE says people are currently diagnosed with home respiratory polygraphy as the first test. Doctors judge how severe the condition is by counting the breathing pauses in an hour of the sleep study. NICE also says oximetry is not considered as sensitive a test for diagnosis and may overestimate blood oxygen levels in people with black or brown skin.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says losing weight, giving up smoking and drinking less alcohol can help. It also lists mouth and facial exercises, but says many people need a CPAP machine, short for continuous positive airway pressure. It gently pumps air into a mask worn over the nose, or nose and mouth, during sleep. The NHS says it is provided free on the NHS for people who need it, and that it is worth telling the doctor if the mask is uncomfortable. Asthma + Lung UK says the sleep clinic prescribes CPAP and shows people how to use the machine and mask.

Asthma + Lung UK describes CPAP as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe disease. For mild disease it is recommended only if symptoms affect quality of life or other options have not worked.

A mandibular advancement device is another option. It is worn in the mouth during sleep and brings the lower jaw forward. NICE says one can be considered for people who cannot tolerate CPAP or decline it. NICE also says surgery can be considered for severe disease in people who could not tolerate CPAP or such a device despite supervised attempts. The NHS lists surgery such as removing large tonsils.

sections.heading: What problems can untreated sleep apnoea cause?
sections.body:
The NHS says that without treatment, sleep apnoea can contribute to high blood pressure, stroke, type 2 diabetes, heart disease and low mood. Tiredness during the day can also lead to accidents. NHS England says CPAP is not a cure, but if it is used every night it is very effective at reversing the symptoms.

On driving, GOV.UK says a person must not drive if sleep apnoea causes excessive sleepiness, until the sleepiness is under control and any needed treatment is being followed. It adds that people with moderate or severe sleep apnoea with excessive sleepiness must tell the DVLA. GOV.UK says someone with sleep apnoea who does not have excessive sleepiness can carry on driving.

Asthma + Lung UK says it is important to treat obstructive sleep apnoea, for example with CPAP, because this can improve both the sleep apnoea and asthma.

faqs.q: Does CPAP get rid of sleep apnoea?
faqs.a: NHS England says CPAP is not a cure, but if it is used every night it is very effective at reversing the symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea. The NHS says the machine is provided free on the NHS for people who need it. Lifestyle changes such as losing weight can also help. If the mask is uncomfortable, the NHS says it is worth telling the doctor.

faqs.q: Does testing for sleep apnoea mean staying in hospital?
faqs.a: Not usually. The NHS says the tests can usually be done at home, though sometimes an overnight stay in the clinic is needed. Asthma + Lung UK names pulse oximetry and respiratory polygraphy as the main sleep tests. It says a fuller study called polysomnography may be needed if the result is not clear.

faqs.q: Can sleep apnoea affect asthma?
faqs.a: Asthma + Lung UK says people with asthma are more likely to get obstructive sleep apnoea, especially if they are overweight, have reflux or have asthma that is difficult to control. It says the condition can make asthma symptoms worse and increase the risk of an asthma attack. It adds that treating it, for example with CPAP, can improve both conditions.

faqs.q: Can someone with sleep apnoea drive?
faqs.a: GOV.UK says a person must not drive if sleep apnoea causes excessive sleepiness, until the sleepiness is under control and any needed treatment is being followed. People with moderate or severe sleep apnoea with excessive sleepiness must tell the DVLA. Someone without excessive sleepiness can carry on driving. A GP appointment is the usual route to talk about symptoms.

faqs.q: When should someone see a doctor about snoring and tiredness?
faqs.a: The NHS advises a GP appointment for pauses in breathing during sleep, gasping or choking noises at night, or constant tiredness in the day. Because it can be hard to tell whether someone has sleep apnoea, asking a bed partner to watch for symptoms can help. Bringing that person to the appointment is also useful.

aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
aortic-aneurysm.definition: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the aorta, the body's main blood vessel, where it runs through the tummy.
aortic-aneurysm.overview: An abdominal aortic aneurysm, often shortened to AAA, is a bulge in the aorta where it passes through the tummy. It is usually caused by weakening of the aortic wall, and it often causes no symptoms and is found by chance. Men are most at risk, and the NHS offers an ultrasound test to all men when they turn 65. If an aneurysm bursts, it is a life-threatening emergency that needs treatment in hospital as soon as possible.
causes: The aneurysm is usually caused by weakening of the aortic wall.
The British Heart Foundation links it to atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty material in the arteries.
Sometimes it can be caused by an infection, but this is rare.
riskFactors: Being a man aged 65 or over
A close relative who has had an abdominal aortic aneurysm
Coronary artery disease or peripheral artery disease
signs: A bulge of the aorta that shows up on an ultrasound scan of the tummy
In a rupture, sudden severe pain in the tummy or back, feeling faint or clammy, or passing out
complications: The aneurysm can burst (rupture), which causes severe bleeding and can be fatal.
A rupture is a life-threatening emergency that needs treatment in hospital as soon as possible.
aortic-aneurysm.diagnosis: The main test for an abdominal aortic aneurysm is an ultrasound scan of the tummy. A CT scan may be arranged if more detailed information is needed, for example when repair is being considered. When a symptomatic or burst aneurysm is suspected, NICE recommends an immediate bedside ultrasound of the aorta.
aortic-aneurysm.treatment: Small aneurysms are usually watched with regular scans rather than operated on, along with healthy lifestyle changes. Surgery to reduce the risk of bursting may be done if the aneurysm is large, is getting bigger quickly or is painful. The two surgical options are endovascular repair, where a graft is threaded up into the aorta from the groin, and open surgery, where a graft is placed through a cut in the tummy. The NHS says both are equally good at reducing the risk of bursting, but each has its own advantages and disadvantages.

sections.heading: What is an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
sections.body:
An aneurysm is a weakness in the wall of a blood vessel that makes it bulge outwards. When this happens in the aorta where it runs through the tummy, it is called an abdominal aortic aneurysm, also known as AAA or 'triple A'.

Most abdominal aortic aneurysms cause no symptoms, so many are found by chance. Even so, an aneurysm that is left untreated can burst, which causes severe bleeding and can be fatal. This is why scans are used to check on one once it is found.

The NHS says an aneurysm is usually caused by a weakening of the main artery that runs from the heart to the tummy. The exact reason it weakens is often unclear. Smaller aneurysms are usually watched with regular scans, while large ones are generally recommended for surgery, as the treatment section explains.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms, and what are the signs of a burst aneurysm?
sections.body:
An abdominal aortic aneurysm often has no symptoms. If it gets bigger, a person might notice tummy or back ache or a pulsing feeling in the tummy. NHS 111 Wales says these symptoms can be caused by lots of things and do not mean a person has an aneurysm, but it is best to get them checked.

A burst aneurysm is different, because it is a life-threatening emergency. Signs of a rupture can include sudden, severe pain in the tummy or back, feeling faint or clammy, trouble breathing, pale or grey skin, and passing out. The NHS advises calling 999 for these signs, because a burst aneurysm needs treatment in hospital as soon as possible.

NHS hospital leaflets say the caller should tell the ambulance service that the person has an aortic aneurysm, and that the person should not drive themselves to hospital. NICE says that when a burst aneurysm is suspected, the person should be transferred for repair without waiting for a CT scan.

sections.heading: What causes it, and who is at risk?
sections.body:
An aneurysm is usually caused by weakening of the aortic wall. The British Heart Foundation links it to atherosclerosis, which is a build-up of fatty material in the arteries. MedlinePlus also lists atherosclerosis as a possible cause of aortic aneurysm. Sometimes an infection is the cause, but this is rare.

NHS 111 Wales lists the risk factors as being a man aged 65 or over, smoking, high blood pressure and high cholesterol. Having a close relative with an aneurysm also raises the risk, as do coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Conditions such as Marfan syndrome are also on the list.

The NHLBI, a US body, calls smoking one of the main factors that raise the risk of an aortic aneurysm, especially an abdominal one. It adds that in a current smoker the aneurysm may grow more quickly and be more likely to burst. NICE says doctors encourage older men and women to get tested if they are at risk, for example if they smoke.

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed, and what is the NHS screening programme?
sections.body:
The main test for an abdominal aortic aneurysm is an ultrasound scan of the tummy. The probe is pressed gently on the tummy, and the scan shows whether an aneurysm is present and how big it is. A CT scan may be arranged if more detailed information is needed.

In England, the NHS offers an ultrasound test to all men when they turn 65, because men are most at risk. The scan is done once unless an aneurysm is found. The NHS says the result is given at the end of the scan and the GP surgery is sent the results. A man whose scan finds no aneurysm is discharged from the programme, and a large aneurysm developing afterwards is described as very rare.

A small aneurysm needs no treatment at that stage because the chance of it bursting is lower, and the man is invited back for a scan every year to check its size. The programme aims to reduce deaths from burst aneurysms through early detection, monitoring and treatment. It does not screen women, because there is currently no evidence to support screening them. NICE says men who have not been screened can be told about the NHS programme and can refer themselves.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on the size of the aneurysm and on whether it is growing quickly or is painful. Small aneurysms are usually watched with regular scans and healthy lifestyle changes rather than operated on. NICE says people being monitored are given advice to improve their health and slow the aneurysm growing, including lifestyle advice.

Surgery is generally recommended for large aneurysms, and may also be considered if an aneurysm is growing quickly or is painful. In endovascular repair, a graft is threaded up into the aorta from a blood vessel in the groin. In open surgery, the graft is placed through a cut in the tummy.

The NHS says both techniques are equally good at reducing the risk of an aneurysm bursting, but each has its own advantages and disadvantages. NHS hospital leaflets describe endovascular repair as generally involving fewer complications and a shorter hospital stay, while open surgery generally needs less long-term follow-up. The choice is usually made together with the surgeon.

faqs.q: Does every abdominal aortic aneurysm burst?
faqs.a: No. Most abdominal aortic aneurysms cause no symptoms and are often found by chance. However, an aneurysm can burst, which causes severe bleeding and can be fatal. This is why small ones are watched with regular scans, while large ones are generally recommended for surgery.

faqs.q: Who is offered NHS screening?
faqs.a: In England, the NHS offers an ultrasound test to all men when they turn 65, because men are most at risk. The result is given at the end of the scan, and the GP surgery is sent the results. NICE says men who have not been screened can refer themselves, and doctors encourage older men and women who are at risk, for example because they smoke, to get tested.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a burst aneurysm?
faqs.a: Signs can include sudden, severe pain in the tummy or back, feeling faint or clammy, trouble breathing, pale or grey skin, and passing out. The NHS advises calling 999, because a burst aneurysm is a life-threatening emergency that needs treatment in hospital as soon as possible. NHS hospital leaflets say the person should not drive themselves to hospital.

faqs.q: Can an abdominal aortic aneurysm be prevented?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus says an aortic aneurysm may not be preventable, but not smoking or stopping smoking lowers the risk. NICE says people being monitored are given advice to improve their health and slow the aneurysm growing, including lifestyle advice. The NHLBI adds that in a current smoker an abdominal aortic aneurysm may grow more quickly.

faqs.q: What types of surgery are there?
faqs.a: There are two main types: endovascular repair and open surgery. In endovascular repair, a graft is threaded up into the aorta from a blood vessel in the groin. In open surgery, the graft is placed through a cut in the tummy. The NHS says both are equally good at reducing the risk of bursting, but each has advantages and disadvantages, and the choice is usually made with the surgeon.

peripheral-arterial-disease.name: Peripheral arterial disease
peripheral-arterial-disease.definition: A long-term condition in which the arteries that supply blood to the legs become narrowed or blocked, affecting the blood supply and causing pain in the legs.
peripheral-arterial-disease.overview: Peripheral arterial disease, often called PAD, is a long-term condition that affects the blood supply to the legs and causes pain in the legs. It is usually caused by arteries becoming narrowed or blocked, most often by fatty deposits building up in the artery walls, which is called atherosclerosis. The most typical sign is calf pain on walking that settles with rest, although some people have no symptoms. There is no cure, but lifestyle changes and medicine can help reduce the symptoms. The British Heart Foundation notes that PAD also puts people at risk of coronary heart disease and stroke.

Atherosclerosis, where fatty deposits build up in the artery walls
Inflammatory blood vessel conditions such as vasculitis
riskFactors: Smoking, described as the most significant risk factor
signs: A weak or absent pulse in the leg or foot
Sores on the legs or feet that heal slowly

The GP may arrange tests, such as blood tests and the ankle brachial pressure index, which compares blood pressure at the ankle and arm. When treatment to restore blood flow is being considered, NICE recommends duplex ultrasound as the first imaging test.
peripheral-arterial-disease.treatment: There is no cure for PAD, but lifestyle changes and medicine can help reduce the symptoms. Treatment includes exercise, with supervised exercise programmes recommended by NICE for people with intermittent claudication. Medicines such as low-dose aspirin or clopidogrel may be prescribed to reduce the risk of blood clots, and statins to lower cholesterol. Procedures to restore blood flow, such as angioplasty or bypass, are considered when symptoms are severe or have not responded to other treatment.
peripheral-arterial-disease.prevention: Stopping smoking and managing diabetes are described as part of living with PAD. The British Heart Foundation describes managing risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure to lower the chance of heart attack and stroke, with medicines such as statins, antiplatelets and blood pressure drugs.

The NHS advises seeking non-urgent advice from a GP if leg pain comes on when walking and eases with rest, if pain is constant or worse at night, or if sores do not heal, so a GP appointment is the usual route.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of peripheral arterial disease?
sections.body: The NHS describes peripheral arterial disease, often shortened to PAD, as a long-term condition that affects the blood supply to the legs and causes pain in the legs. The main symptom is leg pain that comes on when walking and eases after a few minutes of rest. This is called intermittent claudication. The British Heart Foundation describes a gripping, cramping feeling in the calves. MedlinePlus also lists numbness or heaviness in the leg muscles during walking or climbing stairs. Other possible signs include hair loss on the legs, shiny or discoloured skin, weakness or numbness, toenails that grow slowly or break easily, and sores on the legs and feet that heal slowly. MedlinePlus says weak or absent pulses in the legs or feet can be found, and the skin may look pale or bluish. The NHS notes that some people with PAD have no symptoms. If the narrowing becomes severe, pain can be constant or worse at night, which doctors call critical limb ischaemia.

sections.heading: What causes it and who is at risk?
sections.body: The NHS says PAD is usually caused by the arteries that supply blood to the legs becoming narrowed or blocked. The main cause is atherosclerosis, where fatty deposits build up in the artery walls and restrict blood flow to the legs. The British Heart Foundation describes the same process in the arteries of the heart as coronary heart disease, and says having PAD puts a person at risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. Less common causes include inflammatory blood vessel conditions such as vasculitis. Smoking is described as the most significant risk factor for PAD. Diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and older age also raise the risk, and the British Heart Foundation also lists obesity. A study partly funded by the British Heart Foundation found smoking and diabetes to be the two leading risk factors for PAD, while cholesterol remained the top risk factor for coronary heart disease.

sections.heading: How is peripheral arterial disease diagnosed?
sections.body: The NHS says a GP who thinks a person might have PAD will look at the legs and ask about symptoms and family history. They may also arrange tests, such as blood tests and a test that measures blood pressure and blood flow in the arms and ankles. This is the ankle brachial pressure index, or ABPI. NICE describes it as the highest ankle pressure divided by the highest arm pressure in each leg. A hand-held Doppler test can show whether a pulse is present and whether blood is flowing to a limb, according to the British Heart Foundation. NICE advises that a normal or raised ABPI alone should not rule out PAD in people with diabetes, because hardening of the arteries can affect the result. When treatment to restore blood flow is being considered, NICE recommends duplex ultrasound as the first imaging test. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography is the next step when more detail is needed, and CT angiography is an alternative when that is not suitable. MedlinePlus, a US source, says no screening test is recommended for people without symptoms.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body: The NHS says there is no cure for PAD, so treatment aims to ease symptoms and lower the risk of further cardiovascular disease. What is used depends on how severe the symptoms are, and it combines exercise, medicines and sometimes surgery. Stopping smoking is central. NICE recommends that a supervised exercise programme is offered to people with intermittent claudication, and the NHS describes supervised exercise as a first step. Most people with PAD are prescribed an antiplatelet medicine such as low-dose aspirin or clopidogrel to reduce the risk of blood clots. Statins are used to lower cholesterol, and blood pressure medicines are used if needed. Revascularisation, meaning treatment to restore blood flow, is considered when symptoms are severe or have not responded to other treatment. The two main options are angioplasty, which widens a narrowed artery with a balloon, and bypass grafting, which routes blood around a blockage. The NHS says angioplasty is less invasive, while bypass results are generally longer-lasting. NICE says angioplasty for claudication is offered only when imaging confirms it is suitable, advice on changing risk factors has been given, and supervised exercise has not improved symptoms.

sections.heading: What are the complications and when should someone get help?
sections.body: PAD is linked to coronary heart disease and stroke, so treatment also aims to lower the risk of these. The NHS says that if symptoms develop quickly or get suddenly worse, this could be a sign of a serious problem needing immediate treatment. The British Heart Foundation advises calling NHS 111 or 999 in that situation. NHS Scotland guidance lists sudden limb pain, a pale or cold limb, loss of pulse, numbness and weakness or paralysis as reasons to go to A&E or call 999 straight away. Symptoms that come on slowly are usually raised at a GP appointment, and the NHS advises seeking non-urgent advice if leg pain comes on when walking and eases with rest, if pain is constant or worse at night, or if sores do not heal. Both angioplasty and bypass surgery carry a risk of serious complications, and the NHS says this risk is similar for the two. NHLBI, a US institute, describes PAD as a lifelong condition and says a person sees a healthcare provider who specialises in vascular diseases regularly. Quitting smoking can reduce symptoms and the risk of complications, according to NHLBI.

faqs.q: Can peripheral arterial disease be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for PAD, so treatment aims to ease symptoms and lower the risk of further cardiovascular disease. Lifestyle changes and medicine can help reduce the symptoms. Procedures such as angioplasty or bypass may be considered when symptoms are severe or have not responded to other treatment.

faqs.q: What does intermittent claudication feel like?
faqs.a: The NHS describes leg pain that comes on when walking and eases after a few minutes of rest. The British Heart Foundation describes a gripping, cramping feeling in the calves. MedlinePlus also mentions numbness or heaviness in the leg muscles during walking or climbing stairs. The medical term is intermittent claudication.

faqs.q: Can someone have PAD without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS and MedlinePlus both say some people with PAD have no symptoms. The same artery build-up can affect other arteries, and the British Heart Foundation says having PAD puts a person at risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. For that reason, treatment also aims to lower those risks.

faqs.q: How do doctors check for PAD?
faqs.a: The NHS says a GP will look at the legs, ask about symptoms and family history, and may arrange tests such as blood tests and a test comparing blood pressure in the arms and ankles, called the ankle brachial pressure index. If treatment to restore blood flow is being considered, NICE recommends duplex ultrasound as the first imaging test.

faqs.q: When is PAD an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says that if symptoms develop quickly or get suddenly worse, it could be a sign of a serious problem needing immediate treatment. The British Heart Foundation advises calling NHS 111 or 999 in that case. NHS Scotland guidance lists sudden limb pain, a pale or cold limb and loss of pulse as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.
